verdicts.why: Plain verb of saying; choosing it over 'say' or 'inform' says nothing about the speaker's attitude to what is told.
Neutral verb for giving an account; no approval or contempt attaches to the telling or the teller.
The sense of excess is the word's meaning, not an attitude beyond it; 'too angry' states a degree past a limit the way 'huge' states size.
Pure additive adverb, interchangeable with 'also'; nothing to judge.
A bare quantifier of degree or amount; no stance toward the thing quantified.
Reports arriving at a belief; the grounds may be vague but the word takes no side about the belief or the believer.
Neutral verb of establishing a result; it neither approves nor dismisses what is found.
Coming upon something is described without any attitude toward it.
The judgement in 'a hurried manner' or 'an honourable manner' lives in the modifier; 'manner' itself only names the how.
A way of behaving can be good or affected, but that is said by 'good' and 'affected'; the noun is a neutral holder for the description.
Archaic 'all manner of' means simply 'kind'; dated in register but not evaluative.
Reports how someone regards a thing without the word itself endorsing or doubting that judgement.
Accepting as true is stated flatly; unlike 'credulous' or 'swallow', it implies nothing about how wise the acceptance is.
States confidence in something without approval or contempt for the confidence or its object.
Departing from a place is described in the plainest available word; 'flee' or 'abandon' would judge, 'leave' does not.
Entrusting something to another is stated without any view of whether that was wise or kind.
Removing oneself from an association is neutral; the reproach in 'left all her friends' comes from the surrounding sentence, not the verb.
A concessive connective; it steers the argument but takes no attitude toward any person or thing.
Marks a contrast and nothing else; no approval or dismissal is carried.
'To whatever degree' is a purely logical quantifier over extent; nothing is judged.
'At any time' is a temporal quantifier with no attitude attached.
'At all times' describes frequency plainly; it neither praises nor blames what is constant.
'Ever so' is an informal or dated intensifier, a matter of register and strength rather than of judgement toward the thing intensified.
A plain kinship term; 'mother' itself carries no stance, and any warmth or resentment in the sentences is supplied by 'dear' or 'resentfully'.
Addressing an unrelated old woman as 'mother' rather than 'madam' presumes a homely familiarity that marks her as old and humble, affectionate at best and patronising at worst.
